description:
We are Halley's Comet, a passionate and multidisciplinary team of innovators who participated in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, working on the challenge Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data.

Our team is driven by curiosity, creativity, scientific exploration, and a shared passion for using technology and space science to solve real-world problems. We are particularly interested in space exploration, artificial intelligence, data science, engineer
summary:
FlameLens AI is an interactive, SI-powered dashboard that helps mission designers identify the NASA combustion experiments most relevant to fire safety in their mission environment. Built from 31 combustion investigation records in NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and NASA Glenn combustion-science resources, it covers BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE, and FM2.

For each investigation, FlameLens AI records fuel type, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity conditions, measured variables, and whether the research supports fire prevention, detection, or suppression. Users select a mission environment—Spacecraft, Moon Base, or Rover—and the dashboard ranks experiments using a transparent 100-point relevance score based on atmosphere, safety area, fuel type, and gravity.

Each result includes a plain-English summary, a fire-safety insight, and a direct link to its PSI source. Insights are AI-assisted and reviewed by the team. An oxygen–pressure chart highlights experiments closest to expected lunar conditions, while an evidence-gap view shows where partial-gravity combustion data is still missing.

This matters because future lunar habitats and pressurized rovers are expected to operate in oxygen-rich, low-pressure environments, where materials may burn more easily. FlameLens AI turns complex PSI data into clear, source-linked safety insights, helping teams make earlier and better-documented fire-safety decisions for human space exploration.
details:
FlameLens AI is an interactive, SI-powered web dashboard that helps mission designers, aerospace engineers, researchers, and students identify the NASA combustion experiments most relevant to fire safety in their mission environment.

Users select a mission context—Spacecraft, Moon Base, or Rover—and specify conditions such as oxygen concentration, cabin pressure, gravity, and airflow. FlameLens AI then ranks 31 combustion investigation records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and NASA Glenn combustion-science resources using a transparent 100-point relevance score. The score considers atmosphere, safety area, fuel type, gravity, and the relevance of each investigation to the selected environment.

The dashboard covers investigations including BASS, Saffire, SAME, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE, and FM2. For each result, it provides the investigation objective, fuel type, test conditions, measured variables, safety domain, plain-English summary, fire-safety insight, confidence level, and a direct link to the PSI source. Results are classified as Prevention, Detection, or Suppression, helping users quickly understand how each experiment supports a different part of spacecraft fire safety.

A key creative feature is FlameLens AI’s environment-first approach: instead of requiring users to search individual experiments, they begin with their mission environment and receive ranked, source-linked insights. An oxygen–pressure chart highlights investigations closest to expected lunar-habitat conditions, while an evidence-gap view makes clear that partial-gravity combustion data is not yet available in PSI. This prevents overconfidence and helps users distinguish direct evidence from extrapolation.

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive front end, with Chart.js for data visualization. The team used a structured dataset derived from NASA PSI and NASA Glenn resources, with AI assistance used to draft plain-language summaries and insights, followed by team review for accuracy and clarity.

FlameLens AI is important because future lunar habitats and pressurized rovers are expected to use oxygen-rich, low-pressure atmospheres, where materials may burn more easily than on Earth. By making complex PSI data easier to find, compare, and interpret, the project supports earlier material-selection decisions, better safety planning, and more informed research priorities for human exploration of the Moon, Mars, and beyond. It is a decision-support tool—not a certified safety analysis—and every insight is designed to remain transparent, source-linked, and scientifically responsible.
